rv.q: Insipid and shallow play about brothers at opposite ends of America'

Hit Machine is ultimately a show about music without much music at all – only one song is performed in its entirety – and it is a text about weighty themes which it is too eager to resolve rather than allowing its drama to be properly felt and earned.

Funny, insightful and emotionally satisfying, Hit Machine proves that while there may be no guaranteed formula for creating a hit record, Jonathan Caren has come remarkably close to creating a hit play.
Overall, Hit Machine is the perfect show for music buffs, delving deep into what it takes to make a smash hit and create a song with soul.
The music industry is laid out loud and clear, with the night ending in a concert-style performance by Defy that gets the audience rapping along.
The music is vibrant and powerful and lifts the play beyond the familiar clichés.
Radnor and Galvin work well together to fill those gaps, delivering honest portrayals of two damaged souls struggling to regain something long since lost.
The dark, creepy relationship between the three creatives has a lot of potential.

Taken as a whole, Hit Machine works though: the luxury casting of the two American leads really pays off, Madovi feels like a star in his own right, the show looks great, and the musical aspect is fascinating.

This is a fun play; there’s plenty of laughs along the way, including a particularly funny analysis of Call Me Maybe which I’ll be using the next time I talk about music, but there’s also a real intensity to the drama towards the end and a fragility which is moving.
Hit Machine is funny, sharp and poignant.
Hit Machine was still music to my ears, leaving me in no doubt that this production is a huge hit.
It's a thoughtful and thought-provoking production that's worth seeing.
Hit Machine is an impressive play which works well.
It's smart, funny and bursting with songs.
Caren's 'Hit Machine' is sure to rise up the charts.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this music industry drama about feuding brothers. The performances by Radnor and Galvin earn widespread praise, but some find the writing shallow while others appreciate its sharp exploration of family trauma and creativity.
